extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; general educated public interested in science, education, law, and literary/cultural debate (late 19th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative standards and criteria embedded in a popular-science magazine issue containing scientific sketches, an obituary/biographical sketch, and letters on pedagogy, law, suicide, and copyright. Includes standards for teaching, legal distinctions, scientific merit, and explanatory/experimental practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of suicide / legal-ethical criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Suicide is characterized by the intention to take one's own life; to constitute suicide there must be criminal motive — 'felo de se' — self-murder; distinguish suicide from voluntary death performed to save life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: 'Suicide is characterized by the intention to take one's own life. ... To constitute suicide there must be criminal motive, just as in the case of any other crime. It must be felo de se; in its simplest statement, self-murder.' Anti-patterns/examples: voluntary death intended to save others (heroes, martyrs, engineers) is not suicide; 'altruistic suicide' is rejected as a valid ethical or legal category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-defense versus vengeance (criminal-law standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person acting upon a reasonable apprehension of immediate personal danger (e.g., shooting a midnight intruder attempting entry) is held blameless; the same action taken after the immediate danger has passed (pursuing vengeance after robbery and escape) is not blameless and may be criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the letter: 'There appears ... to hold a man blameless if he shoot and kill the midnight robber who is merely trying to effect an entrance into his house, but will not hold him guiltless if he take the same sort of vengeance on the robber after he has once entered the house and stolen the goods and escaped with them.' Rationale: immediacy of threat justifies defensive action; after danger ceases, actions are measured as prevention of crime and subject to society's rules against private vengeance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical standard for teaching evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching evolution in college science courses should present 'such an exposition of the facts favoring and seeming to militate against the doctrine as would be suitable to students.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As noted in the correspondence regarding Amherst: evolution was taught in the zoology department with instructors giving balanced exposition suitable to students; textbook selection (e.g., Dana's and Le Conte's texts which accept evolution) and faculty consensus are cited as relevant institutional practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of scientific eminence (attributes of a great scientist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eminence is indicated by a combination of original theoretical work, skill in mathematics, excellence in experiment, controlled imagination, clarity of exposition, pedagogical value, and substantive contributions across subfields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the sketch of James Clerk Maxwell: he is described as 'an accomplished mathematician, an unexcelled experimenter,' with 'vivid imagination' made 'subservient to the conditions of scientific investigation,' 'power of direct and lucid exposition,' valued as a teacher, prolific in papers and contributions (Transactions, Encyclopaedia), author of major works (Electricity and Magnetism), and instrumental in institutional improvement (Cavendish Laboratory). These multiple attributes are presented as the standards by which his scientific greatness is judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method to infer organ function (insect flight example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of manipulative experiments (removal, suppression, or augmentation) to test the function of an organ and thereby infer its role in behavior or mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by insect-flight experiments: 'I have proved by experiment that the balancers act by displacing the axis of suspension. Suppress the balancers, and the flight becomes fatally downward ... attach a tiny weight to his abdomen ... we restore to the insect the power to perform all his aerial evolutions.' The guidance: remove or alter suspected structures and observe changes; add compensatory weights or modifications to test causal hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for copyright/property claims (natural rights vs. legal construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that an author has no 'natural right' to property in his productions; any property right in literary works exists 'so far as the law may choose to create one for him' — i.e., property in books is a legal, not a natural, entitlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted reasoning: 'An author has no natural right to a property in his production... The author, like other people, seeks the pleasure and the profit of having at his own disposal what he produces ... but that does not destroy or diminish the author's desire and claim to be allowed to have at his disposal... to turn it to account.' The editorial response critiques denying moral concepts (justice, right, wrong) as the basis for property claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasive strategies in the copyright debate (appeal to 'delicacy' vs. appeal to 'honesty' or moral right)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct rhetorical/legal approaches to securing copyright: appealing to a national/communal sense of delicacy and honor (moral suasion) versus appealing to legal/moral rights (honesty, justice) as bases for legal protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From discussion: Matthew Arnold suggests appealing to 'the sense of delicacy' in the community rather than claims of natural rights or honesty; editors argue that while appealing to delicacy is legitimate, denying moral/legal concepts undermines the legal case and may strengthen opponents of copyright. Guidance: choose persuasive grounds carefully—relying solely on aesthetic/delicacy appeals risks leaving the matter without firm moral-legal backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for popular scientific exposition / lecturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects and presentation style determine accessibility: condensed treatment and advanced subjects can debar general audiences; lucid direct exposition is valuable but does not automatically make one a 'popular' lecturer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Maxwell's sketch: 'Though possessed of the power of direct and lucid exposition, he was never what is termed a popular lecturer. The subjects he considered, and his condensed form of presenting them, debarred any, save those whose knowledge was sufficiently extended, from following him in his exposition.' Guidance: to be popular, choose accessible subjects and avoid overly condensed presentation; tailor exposition to the audience's background.
